title: Osmosis

blocks.heading: Key points
blocks.text:
| Learn | |
|---|---|
| Osmosis | net movement of water from a dilute to a more concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane |
| Plant cell, more dilute outside | water in, turgid; the wall stops it bursting |
| Plant cell, more concentrated outside | water out, flaccid, then plasmolysed (membrane pulls away from the wall) |
| Animal cell | no wall: swells and can burst, or shrinks and shrivels |
| Words | turgid, flaccid, plasmolysed describe cells; hypotonic, isotonic, hypertonic describe solutions |
| Roots | water enters root hairs by osmosis and moves down a water potential gradient to the xylem |

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: What osmosis is; what it does to plant and animal cells in solutions of different concentration; how it lets roots take in water and keeps soft plant parts firm; and three ways to investigate it.

blocks.heading: Osmosis and water potential
blocks.text: Osmosis is the net movement of water molecules from a dilute solution to a more concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane. Net means overall: water molecules cross the membrane in both directions, but more cross from the dilute side, so water builds up on the concentrated side. The membrane lets water molecules through but holds back larger solute molecules such as sucrose. Biologists describe the same idea with water potential: water moves by osmosis from a region of higher water potential to a region of lower water potential. Water potential depends mainly on how dilute a solution is, and also on pressure. At the same pressure, a dilute solution has a higher water potential than a concentrated one.

blocks.heading: Plant cells in a more dilute solution
blocks.text: In a plant cell the cell membrane is the partially permeable membrane and the cell sap in the vacuole is the solution inside. Put the cell into a hypotonic solution, one more dilute than its cell sap, and water enters by osmosis. The vacuole swells and pushes the cytoplasm against the cell wall. This outward push is turgor pressure, and the wall pushes back. The cell becomes turgid but does not burst, because the wall is strong. In an isotonic solution, with the same concentration as the cell sap, there is no net movement of water and the cell stays the same size.

blocks.heading: Plant cells in a more concentrated solution
blocks.text: Put the same cell into a hypertonic solution, one more concentrated than its cell sap, and water leaves by osmosis. The vacuole shrinks and the cell becomes flaccid, or soft. If water keeps leaving, the cell membrane, with the cytoplasm inside it, pulls away from the cell wall. The cell is then plasmolysed. The space between wall and membrane fills with the outside solution, because the wall lets it through.

blocks.heading: Animal cells have no wall
blocks.text: An animal cell, such as a red blood cell, also gains or loses water by osmosis, but it has no cell wall. In a solution more dilute than its cytoplasm it takes in water and swells, and with nothing to resist the swelling it can burst. In a solution more concentrated than its cytoplasm it loses water and shrinks, becoming shrivelled. In an isotonic solution it keeps its shape. This is why fluids given to patients through a drip have the same concentration as blood plasma.

blocks.heading: Cell words and solution words
blocks.text: Two sets of words are easy to mix up. Turgid, flaccid and plasmolysed describe the cell. Hypertonic, isotonic and hypotonic describe the solution, compared with the cell contents. In an answer about osmosis, use a solution word for the solution and a cell word for the cell.

blocks.heading: How roots take in water
blocks.text: Soil water is usually more dilute than the cell sap of a root hair cell, so it usually has a higher water potential, and water enters the root hair by osmosis. From there water moves across the root towards the xylem, down a water potential gradient. Some of it travels through the cells and some along the cell walls between them. The xylem then carries it up the plant. The gradient can be reversed. If the soil water becomes more concentrated than the root cell sap, its water potential is lower, and water leaves the roots by osmosis: the plant can wilt even though the soil is wet. Adding too much fertiliser is one way this can happen.

blocks.heading: How turgor pressure supports a plant
blocks.text: A young stem of pumpkin or a leaf of spinach has no wood to hold it up. It stays firm because its cells are turgid: water has entered by osmosis, each vacuole has swollen, and the turgor pressure of each cell pushes its contents against its wall. Turgid cells press against one another like tightly packed balloons, and the whole stem or leaf becomes firm. When the plant loses more water than it takes in, the cells become flaccid and the soft parts droop.

blocks.heading: Seeing plasmolysis under the microscope
blocks.text: Peel a thin strip of epidermis from the inside of an onion scale leaf. Mount one piece in a drop of water and another in a drop of concentrated salt solution, add coverslips and leave both for about ten minutes. Under the microscope the cells in water are turgid, with the cytoplasm pressed against the walls. The cells in salt solution are plasmolysed: the cell membrane and cytoplasm have pulled away from the walls. Red onion makes this easier to see, because the coloured cell sap shows the shrinking vacuole. To turn this into an investigation, mount strips in a range of salt concentrations, wait the same time for each, and count the percentage of cells plasmolysed in a field of view.

blocks.heading: Investigating osmosis with potato cylinders
blocks.text: Plan it first. The independent variable is the concentration of the solution; the dependent variable is the percentage change in mass; keep the size of the cylinders, the time, the temperature and the potato the same, and repeat each concentration. Then cut cylinders of potato of the same length and diameter with a cork borer. Blot each one dry and weigh it. Put one cylinder into each of a range of sucrose solutions, for example from 0.0 to 0.8 mol/dm³, for the same time and at the same temperature. Then remove each cylinder, blot it in the same way and weigh it again. A gain in mass means water entered the cells; a loss means water left.

blocks.heading: Worked example: percentage change in mass
blocks.text: A potato cylinder weighs 2.00 g at the start and 2.16 g after 30 minutes in 0.1 mol/dm³ sucrose. The change is 2.16 - 2.00 = 0.16 g. As a percentage of the starting mass, 0.16 ÷ 2.00 = 0.08, and 0.08 × 100 = 8, so the cylinder gained 8%. Percentages let you compare cylinders that started at different masses. If a second cylinder lost mass in 0.3 mol/dm³, the concentration of the cell contents lies between 0.1 and 0.3 mol/dm³: the solution with no change in mass would match it.

blocks.heading: A model cell made of Visking tubing
blocks.text: Visking tubing is a partially permeable membrane. Tie one end, fill the tube with sucrose solution, tie the other end and weigh it. Leave it in a beaker of water. Water enters by osmosis, so the bag swells, becomes firm and gains mass, much as a plant cell becomes turgid. A bag of water placed in sucrose solution does the opposite.

blocks.heading: Making the results trustworthy
blocks.text: Solution left on the surface of a piece of tissue adds mass that the cells did not take up, so blot every piece in the same way before each weighing. One piece can behave unusually, so repeat each concentration and work out the mean. Water moves slowly, so give the tissue enough time in each solution, and keep the time the same for every piece. If an expected change is not seen, think about what else could explain it: too little time, or a solution that is not concentrated enough.

blocks.heading: Where this connects
blocks.text: Osmosis is a special case of diffusion (3.3.1), for water through a partially permeable membrane. Active transport (3.3.3) moves particles the other way, against a gradient. Water uptake by roots continues in Transport in plants (3.7), which explains transpiration and wilting. The skills the investigations use, naming the independent, dependent and controlled variables, setting out a results table and working out a percentage change, are taught in Scientific processes (1.1 and 1.2).
